Kant: Grounds for Metaphysics of Customs

The video explains the Grounding of the Metaphysics of Customs, by Immanuel Kant, in six steps: pure morality, goodwill, duty, categorical imperative, humanity as the end and kingdom of ends. It ends with the difference between price and dignity and a question: what world do we legislate with our daily choices?

The question: what makes a moral action

The video presents the Grounds for Metaphysics of Customs, by Immanuel Kant, as an attempt to create an absolute moral basis for everyday choices 00:13. This base goes beyond flexible rules and passenger instincts 00:22.

The path has six steps, which the video calls ascent by Kant's ethical pyramid 00:31:

  • the search for pure morality 00:35;
  • the value of goodwill 00:38;
  • act only for duty 00:38;
  • the categorical imperative 00:42;
  • humanity as an end 00:45;
  • the kingdom of ends 00:48.

1. Pure morality: an a priori ethics

Kant separates two fields from philosophy 01:00. Empirical philosophy is based on human experience, psychology and anthropology, and these things are subjective and change all the time 01:06. Pure philosophy demands absolute necessity 01:19.

So a true moral law cannot be based on what people normally do, but on what they should do. 01:24. It is based only on reason and is valid for all rational beings, without exception 01:32.

2. Good will

Intelligence, courage and perseverance are good qualities, but they can become terrible tools if they are not guided by good intention. 01:55. The video sets the example of the calculating criminal: coldness makes him more dangerous 02:03.

So only goodwill is good without condition 02:09. It shines like a jewel with its own value, even if it is neither useful nor practical. 02:15.

The Honest Trader

Kant imagines a merchant who charges fixed and fair prices from all, even from an inexperienced customer or from a child 02:28. The outer action is correct. The question is whether he's morally good or just a smart businessman who doesn't want to lose clients 02:40. An action that seems fair, but is moved by profit and interest, has some moral weight 02:49?

3. Act for Duty

To answer the marketer's dilemma, Kant separates two things 03:02:

  • act according to duty: do the right thing, but waiting for a reward, for ego or for passing sympathy 03:10;
  • acting on duty: the action moved only by respect for moral law, without expecting applause 03:22.

The insensitive philanthropist

The second example is a man who, after the beatings of life, no longer feels compassion or pleasure in helping others 03:31. Still, he helps those who need it, because he understands that moral law requires it. 03:44. For the video, it is when empathy disappears that moral value appears pure: motivation is duty, not emotional comfort 03:51.

4. The categorical imperative

How to find out what is the duty in each situation? The answer lies in the imperatives 04:09:

  • hypothetical imperative: a practical and conditional advice to get what you want. For example, if the goal is to cure a patient, one should give the medicine 04:17;
  • categorical imperative: an absolute commandment, which overrides personal desires and commands an action because it is necessary by itself 04:27.

Before the formula, the video explains the maximum: the personal rule, the internal reason that motivates our decisions without us realizing 04:49. The most famous formulation of the work says that a maxim is only morally correct if it can count for the whole world 05:06. When deciding, you have to want all people in the same situation to make the same choice. 05:16.

Video turns this into a three-step test. 05:29:

1. identify the maxim, the desire behind the action 05:33; 2. Imagine this rule as a universal law of nature 05:38; 3. check whether a logical contradiction arises by universalizing the rule. If it arises, action is dismissed, because it cannot be moral law 05:46.

5. Humanity as an End

Kant translates this law into a second formulation: every rational being has absolute value in itself 06:08. We must treat humanity, in ourselves and in others, always as an end and never as a means. 06:20. No human being can be used as a disposable tool for others' interests 06:31.

The video applies the idea to someone in debt who promises to pay a loan knowing he won't keep it 06:44. The work brings four examples that test the imperative, and the video comments three of them. 06:56:

  • the false promise: who borrows becomes a mere tool, or, in the image of the video, an ATM. And if the false promise became universal law, no one would believe anything and trust would cease to exist 07:00;
  • the talents themselves: abandoning them goes against the natural development of the human being 07:19;
  • help those who need it: denying it ignores that we are all ends in ourselves and need support 07:26.

6. The Kingdom of Ends

The top of the pyramid is the realm of ends: a community of rational beings guided by common moral laws, created by themselves by reason 07:42. In this ideal, each person respects himself and others as absolute ends 07:58.

Hence the conclusion on price and dignity. Everything that satisfies our inclinations, like goods and goods, has a price and can be exchanged for something like that. 08:13. A human being capable of thinking, having autonomy and using his own moral reason is priceless 08:25. He has dignity, which is unconditional and irreplaceable 08:35.

The final reflection

The video closes with a mental experiment. If each choice must obey a rule that could become universal law, which world we are legislating with the attitudes of every day 08:50? ? Understanding the weight of moral autonomy itself is an invitation and a challenge to reassess the choices that shape our lives 09:09.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between acting on duty and acting on duty?

Acting according to duty is doing the right thing waiting for something in return. To act for duty is to act only out of respect for moral law 03:10.

What is the categorical imperative?

It is an absolute commandment: a maxim is only morally correct if it can be used as a universal law for all 05:08.

What's the difference between price and dignity?

What's priced can be exchanged for something else. The human being, capable of reason and autonomy, has no price: it has dignity 08:35.

Reviewed by Maurício Yokoyama Issei in 14 November 2026.

About the video

What makes a truly moral action? In this explanatory video, you will understand the central ideas of the work ** Fundamentation of Metaphysics of Customs ** by Immanuel Kant, an indispensable text to understand the ethics of duty and modern philosophy.

We approach in a didactic way the path outlined by Kant to identify and fix the supreme principle of morality:

**In this video you will see:**
* ** The Good Will:** because it is the only thing that can be considered good in itself, without restriction.
* **Act by duty vs. according to duty:** the crucial difference between acting by calculation, convenience or inclination and acting by pure respect for moral law.
* ** The Categorical Imperative:** the universal principle of practical reason — act only on a maxim that you may want to become universal law.
* ** Humanity as the End in Himself:** the duty to treat every human being always as an end and never as a mere means.
* **Autonomy and Kingdom of the Ends:** human dignity based on the ability of reason to legislate for itself.
